title: SLA-driven interleaving preemptor for continuous batches with KV locality preservation
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Summary:
We need a preemption policy that can (1) enforce tenant SLOs (p99 latency/target tail), (2) maintain throughput for best-effort tenants, and (3) avoid unnecessary KV cache churn that regresses quality. Current hard-preempt approach (evict whole slices and cold-start warmups) causes KV locality loss for interactive tenants and spikes in user-facing latency.

Goal:
Design and implement an SLA-driven interleaving preemptor that slices running continuous batches into fine-grained interleaving quanta, preserves KV locality for hot prefixes, and uses an adaptive preemption budget per-tenant derived from SLO headroom and historical KV residency. The preemptor should be incremental, observable, and safe to roll out as a runtime feature flag.

Key ideas / design decisions:
- Interleaving quanta instead of slice eviction: rather than evicting the whole micro-slice for a higher-priority request, we temporarily interleave the higher-priority request into the next N tokens of an active slice. This reduces KV eviction frequency and latency spikes.
- KV locality preservation score: maintain a moving score per tenant/prefix that estimates hotness and rewarm cost (based on observed cache hit ratio, past rewarm time, and model-specific KV size). Use the score to bias preemption decisions — avoid evicting prefixes with high preservation scores unless SLO breach is imminent.
- SLO headroom-based budget: compute per-tenant preempt budget = f(target_latency, observed_pxx_latency, active_requests). Budget governs how many interleaving quanta or full preemptions a tenant can trigger in a minute.
- Opportunistic eager-split: for slices with mixed-tenancy where KV locality is similar across tenants, perform non-destructive logical interleaving (no KV eviction) to maintain throughput.
- Memory pressure gating: if GPU memory pressure exceeds threshold (configurable), switch from interleaving to more aggressive partial-eviction with prioritized rewarm scheduling.
- Backoff & cooldown: tenants that frequently trigger preemption backoff exponentially to preserve system stability and avoid thrash.
- Fallback policy: when interleaving fails (e.g., cannot meet latency SLO within budget), fall back to classic preemption with best-effort KV rewarm prioritization.

Algorithm (high-level):
1) On arrival of a high-priority request R for tenant T, compute SLO_headroom(T) and KV_preservation_score(T, prefix).
2) If SLO_headroom > safety_margin and KV_preservation_score high => schedule interleaving quantum Q into next running slice(s).
3) Otherwise, if memory_pressure < threshold => attempt partial-evict of least-hot prefix(s) with bounded rewarm budget.
4) If neither possible, enqueue for immediate dedicated slice (expensive) and record metric.
5) Update per-tenant preempt budget and cooldown timers.

Telemetry and observability:
- New metrics: preempt_attempts_total, interleave_success_rate, kv_evictions_by_tenant, avg_rewarm_time, p99_latency_post_preempt, preempt_budget_utilization.
- Dashboards: per-tenant preempt cost (tokens + rewarm seconds), heatmap of KV_preservation_score across prefixes, rollout comparisons vs control.
- Traces: attach preemption decision spans to request traces and slice lifecycle spans.

Implementation plan / milestones:
- Phase 1 (Spike, 1 week): prototype interleaving scheduler in local dev runtime, simulate KV hit-rate tradeoffs with synthetic traces.
- Phase 2 (Engine, 3 sprints): implement preemptor core, preservation scorer, and memory pressure gating; add feature flag + config knobs. Unit tests for budget accounting and cooldown.
- Phase 3 (Canary, 2 weeks): deploy to staging and low-traffic shard; run A/B comparing p99 and model output quality degradation.
- Phase 4 (Rollout): incremental rollout with automatic rollback on QoS regressions (integrate with console alerts).

Testing and acceptance criteria:
- No customer-facing p99 regression > 10% for tenants in control group during canary.
- KV_evictions_by_tenant reduced by >= 25% for interleaving-enabled shards on representative workloads.
- Preempt decision correctness validated by e2e traces and unit tests.

Rollout considerations / fallbacks:
- Feature-flagged by tenant and by cluster. Default off for Dedicated customers until validated.
- Ability to pin tenants to legacy preemption.
- Clear dashboard and auto-rollout abort on energy-of-eviction anomalies.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Granularity of interleaving quantum (tokens vs micro-ops) — smaller quanta reduce eviction but increase scheduling overhead.
- How to model multi-tenant KV sharing where warmup benefits are asymmetric.
- Cost accounting for rewarm (how to bill/attribute rewarm GPU cycles to triggering tenant).

- Prototype perf runbook: https://docs.redwood.ai/dev/kv-interleave-spike.md
- Draft PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4982
- Canary dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/preemptor/canary-100120
